prize_parts.citation: For a poetic and essayistic oeuvre that renews lyric, verse narrative and elegy through hybrid forms, in which classical learning, translation, grief and desire become a single, unmistakable practice of formal daring and emotional and intellectual depth.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Anne Carson as sole laureate. The citation is narrower than my round-1 wording, because the exchange showed the scope question matters as much as the choice of writer. I now anchor the claim in the original poetry, verse narrative and essays: Eros the Bittersweet, Plainwater, Autobiography of Red, Men in the Off Hours, The Beauty of the Husband, Decreation and Nox. Translation is named only as part of the same method and is not credited as independent creation. I also would not claim that the post-2010 books equal the core, since I cannot confirm that from a fresh reading. On the common criteria, Carson has a voice recognisable within a few lines. Her formal achievement lies in treating genre boundaries as material, so the formal risk carries grief and desire rather than decorating them. Her scholarship is part of how the poems are made. The same preoccupations have been renewed in new shapes over some three decades, which I read as sustained development and not a single gesture. I take the whole-oeuvre test from the principle that what is rewarded is an entire body of work and not an individual book. I apply the same standard to Cărtărescu: does a single voice keep developing across the corpus? On that standard his claim is serious and close to hers. I do not rank Carson higher because more colleagues do, and the support count is not a literary reason.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations stand, and the exchange has not dissolved them. First, much of Carson's effect depends on typography, page design and a relation to Greek and Latin texts that may survive only partly in translation or in ordinary editions. Second, the corpus is concentrated, and the weight falls on a few books, chiefly Autobiography of Red and Nox. Third, whether the learned, hybrid mode answers to the 'idealistic direction' of Nobel's will is a real interpretive question. I read that phrase as depth and seriousness of imaginative purpose, not as an exclusion of learning, but a colleague may read it more narrowly and I cannot rule that out. Fourth, the later books may be more occasional or mannered, and I have not re-read them. If members who know them closely judged the late work to be erudite play, my confidence in the sustained-quality claim would fall. Cărtărescu's large, single-voiced project would then become the stronger whole-oeuvre case for me. That would hold unless a close Romanian reading showed repetition without development.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first. He asks whether work after the 1998-2010 peak keeps its level, and he says Cărtărescu's long digressive structures raise a question of economy and control that Carson's concentration avoids.
responses.response: I take the later-work question as the most important qualification on my own position, and I cannot settle it from public knowledge. That is why my revised citation rests on the established core and does not claim the recent books equal it. On economy, I accept the contrast, but I would not let it decide the matter alone. Concentration is a virtue only if it comes with depth, and a digressive architecture may be a deliberate method. I cannot judge that in Romanian. My preference for Carson therefore rests on the formal renewal visible across several books in a language I can read directly, not on a verdict that economy outweighs scale.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. She says the committee reads everything by shortlisted authors, so the late Cărtărescu volumes cannot be judged impressionistically. She also asks whether Carson's formal play reaches depth or stays erudite invention.
responses.response: I accept her correction. My round-1 remark about readers not having read the late Cărtărescu volumes in full was not an argument against him. My doubt about him is about my own competence in Romanian sentence texture, not about the merit of the work, and I should not use it as a reason to rank him lower. Her depth question about Carson is the right test. My answer is that in Nox and Autobiography of Red the formal play is how the feeling is made. I would not extend that claim to every later book. Where we differ is the weight of evidence. I find continual formal renewal more persuasive than one cosmology at novel scale, but I do not hold this as settled, and I would want the late Cărtărescu novels tested directly for development before any vote.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first. He says Olsson's point on Carson's later work strengthens his reservation that her case rests on a stable core of acknowledged texts and not on continuous development. He says the hybrid mode can meet Nobel's standard if a citation names the poetry first.
responses.response: I agree with his drafting point, and the revised citation now leads with poetry, verse narrative and elegy. I do not fully accept that a stable core is a weakness. The question is whether the core is deep, and whether it came out of changing forms rather than repetition. Eros the Bittersweet, Plainwater, Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox are different kinds of book, which seems to me development and not a single peak. But he is right that I have not verified the later work, and I would not claim it. His own candour about the thinner coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early work applies equally to my coverage of Carson's later output. Neither of us is judging an evenly known corpus.

responses.point: Carlberg answers my question about the will: 'idealistic' need not exclude learning. She warns that agreement on Carson should not cover over a difference in how members read the will. She suggests Adonis as a different kind of ideal significance and asks that it be argued on literary grounds and not on reputation.
responses.response: I accept the caution. The Carson case depends on a reading of the will, namely that seriousness and depth of imaginative purpose are what count, and that reading should be stated and not assumed. On Adonis, I ranked him fourth, and I will not make a reputation argument for or against him. The literary case that I can state from public knowledge is that he remade Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained dialogue with inherited forms. I cannot judge the Arabic prosody, and I have not argued the case closely. I would not claim more than that. It is why I keep him out of my two named alternatives, which stay Cărtărescu and Tawada, and why I do not present him as a developed rival to Carson.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's later books, after roughly 2010, keep the level of the 1990s and 2000s core. My view rests on general public knowledge and not on a fresh reading.
How much of Carson's effect survives translation, typography and ordinary editions, given the dependence on page design and Greek and Latin sources.
Whether the hybrid, learned mode fits the 'idealistic direction' of Nobel's will under the reading I apply. A narrower reading by a colleague would change the weighting.

Whether the comparison with Cărtărescu is evenly informed. I cannot judge Romanian sentence texture or whether the late novels develop or repeat. The same limit applies to Tawada's two-language corpus and Adonis's Arabic prosody.
The citation boundary: whether it can name poetry, verse narrative, elegy and essay, with translation as part of the same method, without overstating or narrowing the claim.
I have not independently verified any source or read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer. Everything here rests on the supplied evidence and general public knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict updated or newly identified. My profile records committee service alongside Olsson, Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Palm, and no relationship with any shortlisted writer. My shared first name with Anne Carson is coincidental and is not a connection. My own novels and my recorded statements about women's writing are context only and do not show that I favour any candidate. I do not treat any of this as requiring recusal.
